analysis.one_liner: Keeps Medicare paying market-based rates for doctor-administered drugs while drugmakers rebate the negotiated-price difference.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 with 46 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2022 drug-price negotiation law, drugmakers must eventually charge Medicare the negotiated "maximum fair price" for selected drugs that doctors administer, like chemotherapy. This bill keeps Medicare paying doctors at the current market-based rate (average sales price plus 6%) and instead makes manufacturers pay a quarterly rebate equal to the gap between that market rate and the negotiated price, with the rebate money going back into Medicare's Part B trust fund. It also sets patients' coinsurance off the negotiated price rather than the higher market price. The patient-facing pieces largely secure savings the negotiated-price system was already set to deliver, while the structural change preserves existing payment margins for prescribers and lets manufacturers satisfy the negotiated price through rebates instead of selling at that price directly.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries getting selected doctor-administered drugs, whose coinsurance would be calculated from the negotiated maximum fair price rather than the higher average sales price. Community oncology practices and hospitals that "buy and bill" these drugs also benefit, because payment stays at average sales price plus 6% instead of shifting to the negotiated price. Manufacturers benefit from a compliance method that leaves list prices and the existing distribution system intact.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare patients on costly infused drugs

how_it_helps.text: Sets beneficiaries' coinsurance for selected Part B drugs at 20% of a negotiated-price-based amount (MFP+6) rather than 20% of the higher market-based payment, which matters for drugs that can cost thousands of dollars per dose.

Requires manufacturers to pay a quarterly rebate equal to the gap between the market-based payment and the negotiated price, deposited into the Medicare Part B Supplementary Medical Insurance trust fund, so Medicare recoups the negotiated savings.
Maintains Part B payment at average sales price plus 6% for selected drugs, so oncology practices and hospitals that buy and administer these drugs keep their current reimbursement structure.
Applies the same civil money penalties used elsewhere in the negotiated-price program to manufacturers that fail to pay the rebates.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of selected drugs pay quarterly rebates equal to the difference between market-based and negotiated prices. The cost shows up indirectly in continued high list prices, which other payers and discount programs use as reference points. Taxpayers and beneficiaries are largely held harmless because rebates return the difference to Medicare.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that nothing requires a manufacturer to actually provide selected drugs at the negotiated maximum fair price other than through the rebate, so manufacturers would keep charging high market prices in the channel while paying the difference back separately — leaving the high prices intact as reference points for Medicaid, 340B discounts, and commercial negotiations.

It replaces a direct lower price with a quarterly reporting-and-rebate bureaucracy: the Secretary must report quarterly unit and payment data, and manufacturers must rebate within 30 days, adding administrative machinery that wouldn't exist if the negotiated price were simply charged.

It preserves a 6% add-on to payment for prescribers and excludes the new rebates from the average sales price calculation, keeping payment tied to higher list-based prices; an honest supporter would acknowledge this favors prescriber economics over a leaner pay-the-negotiated-price approach.

The patient coinsurance relief largely replicates what the negotiated-price regime was already structured to deliver, so the bill's main substantive change is the rebate-based implementation, not a new patient benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine patient benefit — coinsurance computed from the negotiated price — is real for people on expensive infused drugs, but it largely matches what the negotiated-price system already provides, so the bill's true weight is structural: it re-implements negotiated prices through rebates, preserving buy-and-bill margins for prescribers and high list prices for manufacturers while Medicare still recoups the savings. It neither undoes the negotiation nor delivers clearly more for patients than current law; it is best read as an industry- and provider-friendly alternative implementation with a patient-access frame.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Gregory Murphy introduced the bill on July 7, 2025, joined by Rep. Gray and Rep. Dunn of Florida as original cosponsors.
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and no further action has been taken since.
It has attracted 46 cosponsors, 33 Republicans and 13 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet. The bill has not moved, so the negotiated-price rules as enacted remain in force unchanged, and prescribers and manufacturers keep the current-law implementation for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; nothing has moved

for.name: Rep. Gregory Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 46 cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 46 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support on paper.

sides.party_line_note: The 46 cosponsors split 33 Republicans and 13 Democrats, and no vote or recorded opposition exists yet — the bill has simply not moved in committee.

industries.industry: Community oncology practices and hospitals that bill Medicare for doctor-administered drugs
industries.note: The bill keeps their payment at average sales price plus 6% instead of shifting to the negotiated price, preserving buy-and-bill reimbursement on higher market-based amounts. Patients in their chairs get coinsurance relief, so the provider gain and the patient benefit sit side by side in this bill.

industries.industry: Brand-name drugmakers of selected Part B drugs (cancer therapies and biologics)
industries.note: They must pay quarterly rebates equal to the negotiated-price gap, so their net revenue on Medicare sales is similar to selling at the negotiated price, but the text says they never have to actually sell at that price — leaving high list prices intact as the reference point for Medicaid, 340B, and commercial bargaining.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to two committees without a hearing stall for the Congress. This one has bipartisan cosponsors but no committee action so far; its realistic path is staying dormant unless its provisions are folded into a broader Medicare or health package later in the session.
